cues.text:
Imagine stepping outside
tonight and seeing
a Moon twice as wide as the one you know.

Beautiful. Except every tide on
Earth would be pulled 8 times harder.
So what if the Moon was twice as close?

This is The If Engine, where
impossible scenarios get real physics,
and every number is shown on screen.
Today the Moon orbits about
384,400 kilometers away, on average.
We'll halve that, to 192,200 kilometers,
on a neat circular orbit.
Moving it would not be easy.
Bringing the Moon closer means draining

energy from its orbit:
about 3.8 × 10²⁸ joules.

That's roughly what the entire Sun
radiates into space in 100 seconds.
Not a job for rockets.
Here's the strange part.

To bring a moon closer,
you'd slow it down.

It would then fall inward, and
end up moving faster than before.
Orbits are counterintuitive like that.
So we'll skip the how.

Our Moon simply arrives in its new
orbit, moving at 1.4 kilometers

per second instead of 1.0, exactly
the speed that orbit needs.

And the first thing anyone
would notice is the night sky.

Today the full Moon spans
about 0.53 degrees of sky.

At half the distance, it spans
1.07 degrees, about twice as wide.

Twice as wide means
about 4 times the area.

Same sunlight, same dusty gray
surface, so the full Moon would shine

about 4 times brighter, roughly 1.5
magnitudes on the astronomer's scale.
It would also race around us.
Kepler's third law shrinks the
orbit to 9.7 days instead of 27.3.

Full Moons would come every
9.9 days instead of every 29.5.

That means the whole show, from a thin
crescent to full and back to dark,
would play out in about a week and a half.

You'd barely finish one
phase before the next began.

Against the stars, it would drift
about 37 degrees a day instead of 13.

In a single hour, it would slide
about 1.4 of its own widths.

And moonrise would slip later
each day by about 2.7 hours,

instead of the roughly
50 minutes we're used to.

And from the Moon, the
view would change too.
Astronauts there would see Earth
spanning about 3.8 degrees instead of 1.9,

a blue world twice as wide
hanging over the horizon.
But the real show would happen in daytime.
Right now, at its average distance,

the Moon looks slightly
smaller than the Sun:
0.527 degrees versus 0.533.

That's why some solar eclipses
today are annular: the Moon doesn't

quite cover the Sun, leaving a thin
ring of fire around a dark disk.

Twice as close, the Moon would look about
twice as wide as the Sun. No more rings.

Every central solar
eclipse would be total.
And the shadow would be enormous:
a dark spot about 1,700 kilometers across,

sweeping over the ground, wide enough
to cover a whole country at once.
Now for the part that really matters.

Tides don't come from
the Moon's pull itself,

but from the difference in pull between
Earth's near side and its far side.

That difference shrinks
with the cube of distance.

Halve the distance, and it grows
by two cubed: 8 times stronger.

Notice the twist. The Moon's direct pull
on Earth only gets 4 times stronger,

because gravity falls with
the square of distance.

Tides double that, because
they depend on how quickly

the pull changes from one side
of the planet to the other.

In the open ocean, the Moon's tide
today is a gentle bulge about 36

centimeters high, in the idealized
case where water responds freely.

Twice as close, that bulge becomes
about 2.9 meters, and the swing from

high to low tide grows from about
54 centimeters to about 4.3 meters.
The timing shifts too.

Because the Moon moves
faster across our sky,
high tide would arrive about every
13.3 hours instead of every 12.4.
But nobody lives in the open ocean.

People live at the edges,
where the water meets the land.

Real coastlines turn that gentle
bulge into something wilder.

Bays and gulfs can resonate with the
tide, like water sloshing in a bathtub.

That's how the Bay of Fundy gets
some of the highest tides on Earth.

Harbors, river mouths,
wetlands and coastal

cities are all shaped
around today's tides.

Every one of them would be forced
by a tide 8 times stronger,
about every 13.3 hours, without a break.

So how high would Fundy's
tides go with 8 times the push?

Honestly, that needs an ocean
model, not a calculator.

Resonance can amplify or dampen,
and the answer changes bay by bay.
What we can calculate is the rhythm.

Today the Sun adds a tide about 46
percent as strong as the Moon's.

When they line up, we get
extra-high spring tides.

With the Moon twice as close, the
Sun's share drops to about 6 percent.
In the simple theory, spring tides today

are about 2.7 times
the size of neap tides.

In the new world they'd be
only about 12 percent bigger.
The monthly rhythm almost vanishes.

Wait. If Earth pulls harder on the Moon
too, could the Moon get torn apart?

There is a limit for that,
called the Roche limit.
Inside it, a moon held together only by

its own gravity gets
pulled apart by tides.

For Earth and our Moon, it's
about 18,000 kilometers.

Our new orbit is still about
10 times farther out than that.
The Moon would be safe.
Earth would pay a price, though.

The tidal bulges drag on our
spinning planet like a brake,
and that slowly lengthens the day.
This isn't hypothetical physics.

The same tidal brake has been
slowing Earth for billions of years.

It's the reason the day keeps
getting very slightly longer.

That braking depends roughly on the
Moon's distance to the sixth power.

Halve the distance, and it
gets about 64 times stronger.
Tidal friction should be adding about
2.3 milliseconds to the day every century.

Twice as close, that becomes about
150 milliseconds per century.

Over a million years, that's about
25 extra minutes per day instead of

about 23 seconds, if the rate stayed
constant, which it wouldn't exactly.
There's a flip side.

The same tidal tug that slows Earth
also pushes the Moon gently outward.

Our real Moon is drifting away
by about 3.8 centimeters a year.

A closer Moon would be
pushed outward harder,
slowly undoing part of our experiment.

And you? Would you feel lighter
with that giant Moon overhead?
For a 70 kilogram person, the extra tidal

pull changes your weight
by about 0.06 grams.
That's less than a tenth of a gram.
Today it's about 0.008 grams.
Tides need size to work.
Across Earth's 12,742 kilometers,

the Moon's pull changes
enough to lift whole oceans.

Across a human body, the difference
is far too small to feel.
So, a Moon twice as close:

about 4 times brighter, a
full Moon every 9.9 days,

only total eclipses,
tides 8 times stronger,
and days stretching about 64 times faster.

Distance is the quiet
number behind our sky,

our oceans, and even
the length of our days.

Change it by half, and
almost everything we

take for granted about
the Moon changes with it.

Every number here came
from a calculation or

a cited source, all listed in
the description. Check our math.
Next time, we leave Earth entirely:

how long could you survive on
every planet in the solar system?
Subscribe so you don't miss it.
This was The If Engine.
Run the impossible. Do the math.
